problems.title: Return owned text
problems.description_md:
A function that builds new text inside its body cannot return a reference to that text: the local `String` is dropped when the function returns, and a reference to it would dangle. The compiler rejects that with E0515, and no lifetime annotation can fix it, because annotations describe how long references live; they never make a value live longer (Book ch. 10.3, "Relationships", and L10.6 Screens 5–6). The fix is to return the owned `String` itself, which moves it to the caller.

`decorate(text)` returns `text` wrapped in square brackets, as a new `String`:

- `decorate("rust")` is `[rust]`; `decorate("")` is `[]`.
- The text is copied exactly between the brackets: no trimming, no escaping, no line break.
- The result is owned by the caller and does not borrow `text`, so it stays valid after the caller's input string is dropped.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::decorate("rust")
Expected:   "[rust]".to_string()
The input goes between brackets in a new `String`.

Expression: crate::decorate("")
Expected:   "[]".to_string()
Empty text gives just the two brackets.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- Return an owned `String`; `Box::leak`, `'static` and `unwrap()` are banned.
hints: The new text is created inside `decorate`, so `decorate` must give it away rather than lend it.
`format!` builds a fresh `String`; returning that `String` moves it to the caller.
`format!("[{text}]")` as the function's result.
problems.solution_approach_md: Build the bracketed text with `format!("[{text}]")` and return it. The return type `String` means ownership moves to the caller, so there is nothing for a reference to outlive.
problems.idiomatic_md: "Return the owned value" is the standard answer to E0515. A `&str` result is possible only when it points into something the caller already owns (P10-18); text created inside the function always comes back as a `String`.

problems.title: Longer borrowed input
problems.description_md:
This is the Book's `longest` function (Book ch. 10.3, "Generic Lifetimes in Functions" and "In Function Signatures"). Without annotations its signature is rejected with E0106: the result is a reference, and the compiler cannot tell whether it borrows from `a` or from `b`. The annotation

```text
pub fn longer<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str
```

says that the result lives no longer than **both** inputs: in practice, as long as the shorter-lived of the two. The annotation does not change how long anything lives; it lets the compiler check every caller.

Implement `longer`:

- Return whichever of `a` and `b` is longer, measured in **bytes** (`len()`), not characters: `"😀"` (4 bytes) is longer than `"abc"` (3 bytes).
- When both have the same byte length, return `a`.
- Return one of the two inputs themselves, not a copy: the result points at the same bytes as the chosen argument. Nothing is allocated.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::longer("rust", "go")
Expected:   "rust"
`rust` has 4 bytes and `go` has 2.

Expression: crate::longer("ab", "xyz")
Expected:   "xyz"
`xyz` is longer, so the second argument comes back.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Each input is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- No allocation (`to_string`, `String`, `format!`, `clone`); `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: `len()` on a `&str` counts bytes, which is the measure this function uses.
Return `a` when it is at least as long as `b`; that `>=` also settles ties.
`if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Compare `a.len()` with `b.len()` and return `a` when it is greater or equal, otherwise `b`. Both branches return one of the parameters, so the result has lifetime `'a` as the signature promises.
problems.idiomatic_md: The single lifetime `'a` on both inputs and the output is the simplest honest signature: either input may come back, so the result can be used only while both are alive. The function returns a view, never a copy, which is why it needs a lifetime at all.

problems.title: Choose a borrowed view
problems.description_md:
A lifetime annotation describes every value a function *might* return, not the one a particular call happens to return. `choose(a, b, first)` returns `a` when `first` is `true` and `b` when it is `false`, so its signature has to cover both:

```text
pub fn choose<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str, first: bool) -> &'a str
```

The compiler checks callers against the signature alone (Book ch. 10.3, "Relationships"). Even in a call that passes `first = true`, the result counts as borrowing from `b` too, so the caller may use it only while both `a` and `b` are alive; one compiler probe shows the error when `b` is dropped too early.

Implement `choose`:

- If `first` is `true`, return `a`; otherwise return `b`. Lengths and contents play no part.
- Return the chosen input itself, not a copy: nothing is allocated.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::choose("left", "right", true)
Expected:   "left"
`first` is `true`, so `a` comes back.

Expression: crate::choose("left", "right", false)
Expected:   "right"
`first` is `false`, so `b` comes back.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Each input is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- No allocation (`to_string`, `String`, `format!`, `clone`); `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: The `bool` decides which input to return; nothing about the strings matters.
An `if` expression whose two branches are `a` and `b` already has the type `&'a str`.
`if first { a } else { b }`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Return `if first { a } else { b }`. Both branches have type `&'a str`, so the `if` expression does too, which is exactly the return type.
problems.idiomatic_md: Giving both inputs the same lifetime is the honest contract when either can be returned. A caller that always passes `true` might wish for a looser one, but the signature would then lie for `false`, and the compiler checks only signatures, never the run-time value of `first`.

problems.title: A borrowed excerpt
problems.description_md:
A struct can hold a reference if it declares a lifetime parameter: `struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }` means an `Excerpt` cannot outlive the text its `part` points into (Book ch. 10.3, "In Struct Definitions"). Its methods are written in `impl<'a> Excerpt<'a>`, and their return types show three different lifetime contracts (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision", "In Method Definitions" and "The Static Lifetime"):

- `text(&self) -> &str` has no written lifetime. By the third elision rule, a method with `&self` gives its returned reference the lifetime of the `&self` borrow, so the result may be used only while the `Excerpt` itself is alive.
- `original(&self) -> &'a str` names `'a`, the lifetime of the text the excerpt points into. The result may outlive the `Excerpt` value, as long as the original text is alive.
- `kind(&self) -> &'static str` returns a string literal, which lives for the whole program.

Implement the three methods (`new` is supplied):

- `text` and `original` both return `self.part`, the stored view itself: no copying, no trimming.
- `kind` returns the literal `excerpt`.

No method allocates. The rows check each contract: a result of `original` and of `kind` is used after the `Excerpt` is gone, and a compiler probe checks that the same is rejected for `text`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let e = crate::Excerpt::new("Call me Ishmael"); (e.text(), e.original(), e.kind()) }
Expected:   ("Call me Ishmael", "Call me Ishmael", "excerpt")
Both views return the stored text; `kind` is the fixed literal.

Expression: { let e = crate::Excerpt::new(""); (e.text(), e.original(), e.kind()) }
Expected:   ("", "", "excerpt")
An empty view comes back empty; `kind` does not change.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- The stored text is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- No allocation (`to_string`, `String`, `format!`, `clone`, `Box::leak`); `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: Two of the three methods have the same body; only their signatures differ, and the signatures are supplied.
`self.part` is already a `&'a str`, so it fits both `-> &str` (shortened to the borrow of `self`) and `-> &'a str`.
`text` and `original` return `self.part`; `kind` returns `"excerpt"`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Return `self.part` from `text` and from `original`, and the literal `"excerpt"` from `kind`. The compiler accepts `self.part` for `text` because a `&'a str` can be used where a shorter-lived `&str` is expected; the signature is what makes the caller's view of the two methods different.
problems.idiomatic_md: Elision keeps everyday method signatures short (`text`), and an explicit lifetime (`original`) is written only when callers need more than the default. `'static` belongs on things that truly live for the whole program, such as literals; it is never a way to make a borrowed value live longer.

problems.title: Generic extrema
problems.description_md:
`extrema(values)` finds the smallest and the largest element of a slice in one pass and returns references to both, as `Some((min, max))`, or `None` when the slice is empty. It extends the Book's `largest` (Book ch. 10.1, "In Function Definitions"): the body compares two `T` values with `<` and `>`, so the type parameter needs the bound `T: PartialOrd`, the trait that supplies those operators (Book ch. 10.2, "Trait Bound Syntax").

- If `values` is empty, return `None`.
- Otherwise return `Some((min, max))`, where `min` is a reference to the **first** element that no other element is smaller than, and `max` is a reference to the **first** element that no other element is larger than. With one element, both references point at it.
- Both references point into the caller's slice; nothing is copied.

Because the result borrows from `values`, it cannot outlive the slice's owner; one compiler probe checks that. The tests call `extrema` with `f64` (which is `PartialOrd` but not `Ord`) and with a type that implements only `PartialEq` and `PartialOrd`, so the bound must be exactly `T: PartialOrd`: adding `Ord`, `Copy`, `Clone` or `Debug` makes those rows fail to compile. Strings compare by bytes, so `"z" < "é"`. Inputs never contain `NaN`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::extrema(&[3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
Expected:   Some((&1, &5))
The smallest value is 1 and the largest is 5.

Expression: crate::extrema::<i32>(&[])
Expected:   None
There is nothing to compare, so the answer is `None`.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `values` holds up to 100,000 elements; no element is a floating-point `NaN`.
- The bound is exactly `T: PartialOrd`. `unwrap()`, `.clone()` and sorting are banned.
hints: Keep two references, the smallest and the largest seen so far, and walk the slice once. Both can start at the first element.

Each `value` from `for value in values` is a `&T`, so `value < low` compares without copying. Update `low` and `high` with two separate `if`s, and only on a strict `<` or `>`, so the first of several equal extremes stays.

`if values.is_empty() { return None; } let mut low = &values[0]; let mut high = &values[0];` then, in the loop, `if value < low { low = value; }` and `if value > high { high = value; }`, and finish with `Some((low, high))`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Return `None` for an empty slice. Otherwise start both `low` and `high` at `&values[0]` and loop over `values`. A value strictly smaller than `low` replaces it; a value strictly larger than `high` replaces it. The two tests are independent, so one element can never update both unless the slice has one element. Strict comparisons mean a later equal value never replaces an earlier one, which is how the first minimum and the first maximum are kept. Finish with `Some((low, high))`.
problems.idiomatic_md: Returning `Option<(&T, &T)>` lets one generic function serve every orderable type without copying anything, which is why the bound can stay at `PartialOrd`; the standard library's `Iterator::min` and `max` (Chapter 13) follow the same idea but return the *last* maximum, so the "first of equals" rule here is a choice the spec states, not a default.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` values. For each value draw `k = pick(4)`: 0 gives `pick(11) - 5`; 1 gives `next()` read as an `i32` (two's complement); 2 gives `i32::MIN`; 3 gives `i32::MAX`. Call `crate::extrema(&v)` and compare with the oracle: `None` for an empty vector, otherwise references to the element at the lowest index holding the minimum value and the element at the lowest index holding the maximum value (checked with `std::ptr::eq`). Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000015`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases containing i32::MIN or i32::MAX 278; cases whose maximum occurs more than once 217; cases whose minimum occurs more than once 208; cases with an empty slice 10; cases with one element 10.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Stable borrowed uniqueness
problems.description_md:
`stable_unique(values)` returns one reference for each distinct value in a slice, in the order the values first appear. "Distinct" means "not `==` to an earlier element", so the only capability the function needs is equality: the bound is `T: PartialEq` (Book ch. 10.2, "Trait Bound Syntax"). No sorting, hashing or copying is involved, which keeps the function usable for any type that can be compared for equality (Book ch. 10.1, "In Function Definitions").

- Walk `values` from first to last. Add a reference to an element to the result only if no element already in the result is equal to it.
- The result keeps the order of first appearance and points at the **first** occurrence of each value, not at a later equal one.
- An empty slice gives an empty vector.

The returned `Vec<&T>` borrows from `values`, which the elided signature expresses: with one reference parameter, the output references get its lifetime (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision"). Equality is whatever `==` says for the type: two `f64` zeros of different sign are equal, `"é"` (one scalar) and `"e\u{301}"` (two scalars) are not, and `"Rust"` differs from `"rust"`. Comparing each element only with its neighbour (as `Vec::dedup` does) is not enough: a value can come back after a different one.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::stable_unique(&[5, -1, 5, 2, -1])
Expected:   vec![&5, &-1, &2]
Each value is kept once, where it first appears.

Expression: crate::stable_unique::<i32>(&[])
Expected:   Vec::<&i32>::new()
There are no values, so the result is empty.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `values` holds up to 100,000 elements with at most 2,000 distinct values, so checking each element against the distinct values found so far is fast enough.
- The bound is exactly `T: PartialEq`. `unwrap()`, `.clone()`, `sort`, `dedup` and `HashSet`/`HashMap` are banned.
hints: The result itself is the record of which values you have already seen: before adding an element, look through the references you have kept so far.

Use two loops: the outer one over `values` (each item is a `&T`), the inner one over `&out` (each item is a `&&T`). Compare with `*kept == value`, which compares two `&T`, and remember whether a match was found.
`for value in values { let mut seen = false; for kept in &out { if *kept == value { seen = true; break; } } if !seen { out.push(value); } }` and return `out`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Create an empty `Vec<&T>`. For each `value` in the slice, scan the references already in the result; if one of them is equal to `value`, skip it, otherwise push `value`. Because elements are pushed in input order and only on their first appearance, the result is in first-appearance order and every reference points at a first occurrence. The work is the number of elements times the number of distinct values.
problems.idiomatic_md: With only `PartialEq` available, a linear search through the values kept so far is the honest algorithm; a `HashSet` would need `Eq + Hash` and sorting would need `Ord`, both stronger than the problem allows. Returning references rather than copies keeps the function free of a `Clone` bound and lets the caller see which element was kept.

For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` values. For each value draw `k = pick(5)`: 0 to 2 give `pick(7) - 3`; 3 gives `next()` read as an `i32`; 4 repeats an earlier value, `v[pick(current length)]`, or gives 0 when there is none yet. Call `crate::stable_unique(&v)` and compare with the oracle: the indices of the first occurrence of each value, in increasing order; the result must have that length and each reference must point at that index (`std::ptr::eq`). Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000016`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with repeated values 250; cases where a value repeats after a different value 222; cases with no repeated value 39; cases with an empty slice 11.

problems.title: Generic revision slots
problems.description_md:
A `Slot<T>` holds one value of any type `T` and counts how many times it has been replaced. It is a generic struct (Book ch. 10.1, "In Struct Definitions"), and its methods live in `impl<T> Slot<T>`, so they work for every `T` (Book ch. 10.1, "In Method Definitions"). The struct is supplied; write its two methods:

- `Slot::new(value)` stores `value` with `revisions` set to 0.
- `slot.replace(value)` takes the slot **by value** (`self`), and returns a pair: a new slot holding the replacement `value` with `revisions` one higher than before, and the old value that was in the slot.
- The revision count stops at `u32::MAX`: replacing a slot whose count is already `u32::MAX` keeps it at `u32::MAX` instead of overflowing. (`saturating_add` does exactly this, Chapter 3.)

Because `replace` owns the old slot, it can move `self.value` out and hand it back without copying it (Chapter 4, "Ownership and Functions"). That is why `impl<T>` needs no bound at all: the tests use a type that implements no traits, and a `T: Clone`, `T: Debug` or `T: Default` bound would reject it. The old slot is moved into the call, so the caller cannot use it afterwards; a compiler probe checks that.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::Slot::new(String::from("draft")).replace(String::from("final"))
Expected:   (crate::Slot { value: "final".to_string(), revisions: 1 }, "draft".to_string())
A fresh slot has 0 revisions; after one replacement it has 1, and "draft" is returned.

Expression: crate::Slot::new(7)
Expected:   crate::Slot { value: 7, revisions: 0 }
With `T = i32`, the slot holds 7 and has not been replaced.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `T` is any type; texts are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- No bounds on `impl<T> Slot<T>`. `unwrap()` and `.clone()` are banned.
hints: `replace` owns `self`, so it may take the old slot apart: its `value` field can move straight into the returned pair.

Build the new slot first with the struct literal `Self { value, revisions: ... }`, then return `(next, self.value)`. For the count, `self.revisions + 1` overflows at `u32::MAX`; use the saturating form.
`new` is `Self { value, revisions: 0 }`; `replace` is `let next = Self { value, revisions: self.revisions.saturating_add(1) }; (next, self.value)`.
problems.solution_approach_md: `new` fills both fields with the struct-literal shorthand. `replace` builds the next slot from the replacement value and `self.revisions.saturating_add(1)`, then returns it together with `self.value`. Reading `self.revisions` copies a `u32`; moving `self.value` out is allowed because `self` is owned by the method and is not used again. No value is ever duplicated, which is what lets `T` stay unbounded.
problems.idiomatic_md: Taking `self` by value and returning the old contents is how Rust APIs hand back what they replace (compare `std::mem::replace` and `Option::replace`); it moves values instead of cloning them, so a generic container needs no `Clone` bound. `saturating_add` states the overflow policy in one call instead of an `if`.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `t = text()`, then `k = pick(4)` for the starting count: 0 gives `pick(10)`; 1 gives `next()`; 2 gives `u32::MAX`; 3 gives `u32::MAX - 1`. Then draw `u = text()`. Call `crate::Slot { value: t, revisions: count }.replace(u)` with both texts as `String`s and compare with the oracle `(Slot { value: u, revisions: min(count + 1, u32::MAX) }, t)`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000017`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases already at u32::MAX (saturating) 85; cases at u32::MAX - 1 (reaching the maximum) 82; cases with a small revision count 73; cases with an arbitrary u32 revision count 60; cases whose old value is empty 16.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Partition generic outcomes
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::partition(vec![crate::Outcome::Value("rust"), crate::Outcome::Error(7u32), crate::Outcome::Empty, crate::Outcome::Value("book")])
Expected:   (vec!["rust", "book"], vec![7], 1)
Two values, one error and one `Empty`.

Expression: crate::partition::<i32, String>(Vec::new())
Expected:   (Vec::<i32>::new(), Vec::<String>::new(), 0)
Nothing to sort, so every part is empty.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 100,000 outcomes; texts are valid UTF-8.
- No bounds on `T` or `E`. `unwrap()` and `.clone()` are banned.
hints: Three results means three accumulators: two empty vectors and a counter, filled in one pass.
`for outcome in outcomes` (no `&`) consumes the vector and gives you each `Outcome<T, E>` by value, so a `match` arm such as `Outcome::Value(value) => values.push(value)` moves the payload.
Inside the loop: `match outcome { Outcome::Value(value) => values.push(value), Outcome::Error(error) => errors.push(error), Outcome::Empty => empty += 1 }`; return `(values, errors, empty)`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Create `values`, `errors` and `empty = 0`. Loop over the vector by value, and `match` each outcome: push a `Value` payload onto `values`, an `Error` payload onto `errors`, and count `Empty`. Pushing in loop order keeps each vector in the order the payloads appeared. Return the three as a tuple; Rust infers `Vec<T>` and `Vec<E>` from the return type.
problems.idiomatic_md: Consuming the input (`Vec<Outcome<T, E>>`, not `&[...]`) is what lets the payloads move without a `Clone` bound; a borrowed slice could only hand out references. `match` with one arm per variant also makes the compiler check that no variant is forgotten.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `count = pick(25)`, then `count` outcomes. For each outcome draw `op = pick(3)`: 0 gives `Value(text())` as a `String`; 1 gives `Error(next())` as a `u32`; 2 gives `Empty`. Call `crate::partition::<String, u32>(v)` and compare with the oracle: the `Value` texts in order, the `Error` numbers in order, and the number of `Empty`s. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000018`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases mixing all three variants 212; cases using only one or two variants 71; cases with no outcomes 17.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

- Required: the body of `partition` uses `match`. Banned: `unwrap()` and `.clone()` anywhere in the learner file.

problems.title: Default page reports
problems.description_md:
The trait `PageReport` describes anything that can be printed as a page. It has two required methods, `title` and `lines`, and one method with a default body, `render` (Book ch. 10.2, "Defining a Trait" and "Default Implementations"). A default method can call the required ones, so every implementor gets `render` for free and may still override it. `Page` and its `impl PageReport for Page` are supplied; it returns copies of its own fields.

Write two things:

- The default body of `render`: the title, a line feed (`\n`), then the lines joined with `\n`. With no lines, the result is the title followed by one `\n`; there is no line feed at the end otherwise.
- `render_pages(pages)`: call `render` on every page, in order, and join the results with the separator `\n---\n` (line feed, three hyphens, line feed). An empty slice gives an empty string; one page gives just its render, with no separator.

`render_pages` is generic, `fn render_pages<T: PageReport>(pages: &[T])` (Book ch. 10.2, "Trait Bound Syntax"), so it works for any implementor, including types that override `render`. It must call `render` and use what comes back, not rebuild the text from `title` and `lines`: the tests pass a type whose `render` is overridden. The bound is only `PageReport`; the test types implement nothing else.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::Page { title: String::from("Intro"), body: vec![String::from("one"), String::from("two")] }.render()
Expected:   "Intro\none\ntwo".to_string()
Title, then the two lines, separated by line feeds.

Expression: crate::render_pages(&[crate::Page { title: String::from("A"), body: vec![String::from("x")] }, crate::Page { title: String::from("B"), body: vec![String::from("y")] }])
Expected:   "A\nx\n---\nB\ny".to_string()
Each page renders as two lines; `---` goes between them.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 1,000 pages with at most 100,000 bytes of text in total; titles and lines are valid UTF-8 and may be empty.
- `unwrap()` is banned. The supplied `impl PageReport for Page` stays as it is.
hints:
Both pieces are joins: `render` joins the lines of one page with `
`, and `render_pages` joins whole renders with `
---
`.

Inside the trait, `self.title()` and `self.lines()` work for whatever type implements it. `Vec<String>` has a `join("\n")` method (Chapter 8), and `join` on an empty vector gives an empty string, which handles the no-lines case.

`render` is `format!("{}
{}", self.title(), self.lines().join("
"))`. In `render_pages`, push `page.render()` for each page into a `Vec<String>` and return `parts.join("
---
")`.
problems.solution_approach_md: The default `render` formats the title, a line feed and the joined lines. Because it calls only the required methods, it is valid for every implementor. `render_pages` collects each page's `render()` result into a vector in order and joins it with `\n---\n`; `join` puts separators only between items, so there is no separator for zero or one page.
problems.idiomatic_md: Putting shared behaviour in a default method keeps implementors small (they write only `title` and `lines`) while still letting one type replace it; calling `page.render()` instead of re-deriving the text is what respects such an override. `join` expresses "separator between items" without index arithmetic.

Build the `Page`s and call `crate::render_pages(&pages)`; the oracle renders each page as its title, `\n`, and its lines joined with `\n`, then joins the pages with `\n---\n`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000019`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: pages with no body lines 114; cases with no pages 80; cases with one page 78; cases with two pages 74; cases with three pages 68.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Different trait implementors
problems.description_md:
The trait `Greet` has a required method `name` and a default method `greeting` that builds `Hello, {name}!` (Book ch. 10.2, "Default Implementations"). Two types are supplied: `Person` keeps the default, and `Override` replaces `greeting` with its own `Override: {name}`.

Write `greet_pair(a, b)`, which returns the greeting of `a`, then the three characters ` / ` (space, slash, space), then the greeting of `b`. Its parameters are written `a: &impl Greet, b: &impl Greet` (Book ch. 10.2, "Traits as Parameters"):

- Each `impl Greet` is its own anonymous type parameter, so `a` and `b` may be **different** types: a `Person` and an `Override`, or a type the caller defined. (`fn greet_pair<T: Greet>(a: &T, b: &T)` would force both to be the same type.)
- Call `greeting()` on each value and use exactly what it returns. A type that overrides `greeting` must be greeted its own way, so the function must not rebuild `Hello, …!` from `name()`.
- Names are used as they are: no trimming, no case changes.

The parameters are references, so `greet_pair` borrows its arguments and the caller can keep using them.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::greet_pair(&crate::Person(String::from("Ada")), &crate::Override(String::from("Bob")))
Expected:   "Hello, Ada! / Override: Bob".to_string()
`Person` uses the default greeting; `Override` uses its own.

Expression: crate::greet_pair(&crate::Override(String::from("Bob")), &crate::Person(String::from("Ada")))
Expected:   "Override: Bob / Hello, Ada!".to_string()
Swapping the arguments swaps the two halves.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Names are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes and may be empty.
- `unwrap()` is banned; `greet_pair` must not call `name()`. The supplied trait and implementations stay as they are.
hints: Each value already knows how to greet itself; `greet_pair` only combines two greetings.
Inside the function, `a` and `b` can be used only through the `Greet` trait, and `greeting()` is part of it. Ask each value for its greeting rather than assembling one from `name()`.
The whole body is `format!("{} / {}", a.greeting(), b.greeting())`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Call `a.greeting()` and `b.greeting()` and put ` / ` between them with `format!`. Method calls dispatch to each type's own `greeting`: the trait's default for `Person`, the overriding method for `Override`, and whatever a caller-defined type supplies. Because the parameters are two separate `impl Greet`, the two arguments may be of different types.
problems.idiomatic_md: `&impl Trait` is the short form of a generic parameter with a trait bound; writing it twice gives two independent type parameters, which is what lets one call mix implementors. Delegating to `greeting()` instead of re-deriving the text keeps the function correct for implementors that customise their behaviour.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `t = text()`, `u = text()` and `k = pick(4)`. `k` selects the argument types: 0 `(Person(t), Person(u))`, 1 `(Person(t), Override(u))`, 2 `(Override(t), Person(u))`, 3 `(Override(t), Override(u))`. Call `crate::greet_pair(&first, &second)` and compare with the oracle: each `Person` greets as `Hello, {name}!`, each `Override` as `Override: {name}`, joined with ` / `. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A00001A`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with (Override, Override) 81; cases with (Override, Person) 74; cases with (Person, Override) 73; cases with (Person, Person) 72; cases with an empty name 29.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Conditional ranked pairs
problems.description_md:
`Pair<T, U>` is a generic struct with two public fields of possibly different types. Any `Pair` can be built, but some pairs can also pick a **winner**: when both fields have the same type and that type implements the trait `Ranked`. That is a conditional implementation: the method lives in `impl<T: Ranked> Pair<T, T>`, so it exists only for pairs that meet the bound (Book ch. 10.2, "Using Trait Bounds to Conditionally Implement Methods"). The struct, the trait, the type `Score` and the empty `impl` block are supplied.

Write `winner(&self) -> &T`:

- Compare `self.x.points()` with `self.y.points()`. Return a reference to `self.x` if its points are **greater than or equal to** those of `self.y` (a tie goes to `x`); otherwise return a reference to `self.y`.
- Return the field itself, not a copy; the result borrows the pair, so it cannot outlive it (lifetime elision gives the result the lifetime of `&self`, Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision").
- Compare the points directly with `>=`. Points cover the whole `i64` range, so subtracting them (`x - y`) can overflow.

`struct Pair` itself has no bounds, so a `Pair` of an `i32` and a `&str` is still fine; it simply has no `winner`. The tests use a ranked type defined in the row with no other traits, so the `impl` must not ask for more than `Ranked`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let p = crate::Pair { x: crate::Score { label: String::from("Ada"), points: 7 }, y: crate::Score { label: String::from("Bob"), points: 9 } }; p.winner().label.clone() }
Expected:   "Bob".to_string()
Bob has 9 points, more than Ada's 7.

Expression: { let p = crate::Pair { x: crate::Score { label: String::from("Ada"), points: 5 }, y: crate::Score { label: String::from("Bob"), points: 5 } }; p.winner().label.clone() }
Expected:   "Ada".to_string()
Equal points, so `x` (Ada) wins.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Points are any `i64` values; labels are valid UTF-8.
- No arithmetic on points. `unwrap()` and `.clone()` are banned. The supplied struct, trait and `Score` stay as they are.
hints: Inside `impl<T: Ranked> Pair<T, T>`, both fields are known to be `Ranked`, so you can call `points()` on each.
Decide with one comparison of the two `i64` scores and return `&self.x` or `&self.y`. Use `>=` so a tie keeps `x`; do not compute a difference.
`if self.x.points() >= self.y.points() { &self.x } else { &self.y }`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Read both scores through the trait and compare them with `>=`. Return `&self.x` when it is at least as high, otherwise `&self.y`. Both branches return a reference into `self`, which matches the elided signature `fn winner(&self) -> &T`. Comparing the numbers directly is safe for every `i64`, while subtracting them overflows when the scores are far apart.
problems.idiomatic_md: A conditional `impl` adds behaviour only where it makes sense, instead of putting a bound on the struct and making every `Pair` pay for it; the compiler then reports a missing method (E0599) for pairs that do not qualify. Returning `&T` lets the caller inspect the winner without moving or cloning it.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw a score for `x`, then one for `y`. For each score draw `k = pick(4)`: 0 gives `pick(7) - 3`; 1 gives `(next() << 32) | next()` read as an `i64` (the first `next()` is the high half); 2 gives `i64::MIN`; 3 gives `i64::MAX`. Build `Pair { x: Score { label: "x", points }, y: Score { label: "y", points } }` and check `std::ptr::eq(p.winner(), &p.x)` against the oracle `x.points >= y.points`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A00001B`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases where y scores higher 128; cases where x scores higher 126; cases where y - x would overflow i64 113; cases with a tie (x wins) 46.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: An independently owned opaque greeter
problems.description_md:
`owned_greeter(text)` makes a greeter from a name typed by a user. Its return type is `impl Greet + use<>`: the caller gets *some* type that implements `Greet` and can call `name()` and `greeting()` on it, but cannot see that it is a `Person` (Book ch. 10.2, "Returning Types That Implement Traits"). The trait (with its default `greeting`), `Person` and its `impl` are supplied.

- Remove leading and trailing whitespace from `text` with `trim()`, which removes every Unicode whitespace character (spaces, tabs, line feeds, the ideographic space U+3000) but nothing else: inner spaces, a NUL character or a combining accent stay.
- Return a `Person` that **owns** the trimmed name as a `String`.

About `+ use<>`: in edition 2024 a returned `impl Trait` is assumed to borrow from every reference parameter, so by default the caller could not drop `text`'s owner while the greeter is alive. `use<>` with an empty list promises that the returned value borrows from no parameter (L10.5 explains this). The promise is checked: returning a `Person` that held a `&str` into `text` would not compile. That is exactly why the name must be copied into an owned `String`: one row drops the input `String` before using the greeter.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::owned_greeter("  Ada ").greeting()
Expected:   "Hello, Ada!".to_string()
The spaces around "Ada" are removed.

Expression: crate::owned_greeter("Bob").name()
Expected:   "Bob".to_string()
Nothing to trim; the name is kept.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `text` is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes and may be empty.
- The return type stays `impl Greet + use<>`. `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: The function returns a `Person`; only its name needs work.
`text.trim()` gives a `&str` view of the trimmed name, but the greeter must not borrow `text`, so turn that view into an owned `String`.
`Person(text.trim().to_string())`.

The `String` belongs to the `Person`, so the returned value borrows nothing, which is what `+ use<>` promises; the caller may drop the original text and keep the greeter.

problems.title: Ordered ID newtypes
problems.description_md:
`Id` is a newtype: a tuple struct around a `u32` that gives ID numbers their own type (Chapter 5). Its comparison traits are derived (`PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord`), so IDs compare by their number. Make it work with three standard traits (Book ch. 10.2, "Implementing a Trait on a Type"; L10.5 covers `Display` and `From`):

- `impl std::fmt::Display for Id`: an ID prints as `#` followed by its number in decimal, such as `#42`, with nothing else. `{}` and `to_string()` then work for `Id`.
- `impl From<u32> for Id`: `Id::from(42)` is `Id(42)`. Implementing `From` also gives `let id: Id = 42.into();` for free. The reverse conversion, `From<Id> for u32`, is supplied.
- `ordered_ids(values)`: turn every number into an `Id`, sort the IDs, and return their `Display` texts in that order. Duplicates are kept. The input slice is not changed.

The order is **numeric**: `#9` comes before `#10`, even though the text `"#10"` sorts before `"#9"`. That is why the sorting happens on `Id` values (using the derived `Ord`) before they are formatted, not on the strings afterwards.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::ordered_ids(&[30, 4, 100])
Expected:   vec!["#4".to_string(), "#30".to_string(), "#100".to_string()]
4 < 30 < 100, so the texts follow that order.

Expression: crate::Id::from(7).to_string()
Expected:   "#7".to_string()
`to_string()` comes from `Display`.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 100,000 values, each any `u32`.
- `unwrap()` is banned. The struct and its derives stay as they are.
hints: There are three small pieces: the text of one ID, the conversion from a number, and a function that uses both after sorting.

`fmt` writes into the formatter with `write!(f, ...)`; `from` just wraps the number. In `ordered_ids`, build a `Vec<Id>` first and call `sort()` on it (the derived `Ord` sorts numerically), and only then format.
`write!(f, "#{}", self.0)`, `Id(n)`, and in `ordered_ids`: push `Id::from(*n)` for each value, `ids.sort()`, then push `id.to_string()` for each `id`.
problems.solution_approach_md: `Display::fmt` writes `#` and the number with `write!`, and `From::from` wraps the number in `Id`. `ordered_ids` converts each input number with `Id::from(*n)` into a new vector (the input slice is borrowed, not changed), sorts that vector with the derived numeric `Ord`, and formats each ID with `to_string()`, which `Display` provides.
problems.idiomatic_md: A newtype with standard traits reads like a built-in type: `{}` prints it, `.into()` builds it and `sort()` orders it. Sorting the typed values before formatting is the general rule: once numbers become strings, their order is lexicographic.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` values. For each value draw `k = pick(4)`: 0 gives `pick(20)`; 1 gives `next()`; 2 gives `u32::MAX`; 3 gives `10` to the power `pick(10)`. Call `crate::ordered_ids(&v)` and compare with the oracle: the values sorted numerically, duplicates kept, each written as `#` and its decimal digits. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A00001D`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases where text order differs from numeric order 240; cases with repeated IDs 217; cases with no IDs 16.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Borrowed lookup boundaries
problems.description_md:
`borrowed_lookup(items, wanted)` searches a slice for the first element equal to `wanted` and returns a reference to that element, or `None`. The signature has two reference parameters, so lifetime elision cannot decide what the result borrows from; it says so explicitly (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Function Signatures"):

```rust
pub fn borrowed_lookup<'a, T: PartialEq>(items: &'a [T], wanted: &T) -> Option<&'a T>
```

- The result has lifetime `'a`, the lifetime of `items`, and `wanted` has a separate, unnamed lifetime. So the found reference must point into `items`, never at `wanted`, and the caller may drop the query value as soon as the call returns.
- Compare with `==` (the bound `T: PartialEq`), in order from the start, and return the **first** match.
- Return `None` when nothing matches, including for an empty slice.

Equality is exactly what `==` says for the type: `-0.0 == 0.0` is true, `NaN == NaN` is false, and `"é"` is not equal to `"e\u{301}"`. The result still cannot outlive the collection itself (Book ch. 10.3, "Preventing Dangling References with Lifetimes"); a compiler probe checks that, and another shows why the annotation is needed at all.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::borrowed_lookup(&[4, 7, 9], &7)
Expected:   Some(&7)
7 is in the slice.

Expression: crate::borrowed_lookup(&[4, 7, 9], &5)
Expected:   None
5 is not in the slice.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `items` holds up to 100,000 elements.
- The signature stays as given. `unwrap()` and `.clone()` are banned.
hints: Walk the slice in order and stop at the first element equal to `wanted`.
`for item in items` gives each element as a `&'a T`, which is exactly what the result needs; `item == wanted` compares two `&T` with `PartialEq`. Return early with `return Some(item);`.
`for item in items { if item == wanted { return Some(item); } } None`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Loop over `items`; each `item` is a reference with lifetime `'a`. When `item == wanted`, return `Some(item)` at once, which makes it the first match. After the loop, return `None`. Returning `wanted` instead would not compile, because its lifetime is not `'a`: the signature itself rules that mistake out.
problems.idiomatic_md: Naming a lifetime only on the parameter the result comes from documents the borrow precisely and gives callers the most freedom: they can pass a temporary as the query. The standard library's `slice::iter().find` (Chapter 13) returns a reference into the slice in the same way.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` values, each `pick(11) - 5`, then the query `pick(11) - 5`. Call `crate::borrowed_lookup(&v, &query)` and compare with the oracle: a reference to the element at the lowest index equal to the query (checked with `std::ptr::eq`), or `None`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A00001E`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases found later in the slice 158; cases not found 103; cases where the wanted value occurs more than once 89; cases found at index 0 26; cases not found (empty slice) 13.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: A word view from two owners
problems.description_md:
`longest_word(a, b)` looks at the words of two texts and returns the longest one, as a view into whichever text it came from. Like the Book's `longest` (Book ch. 10.3, "Generic Lifetimes in Functions"), the signature gives both inputs and the result one lifetime, `'a`:

```rust
pub fn longest_word<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str
```

That tells the compiler the result may borrow from either input, so the caller must keep **both** alive while using it (Book ch. 10.3, "Thinking in Terms of Lifetimes").

- A word is a maximal run of non-whitespace characters, as `split_whitespace()` produces (Chapter 8). Whitespace is any Unicode whitespace: space, tab, line feed, U+3000 and so on. NUL and combining accents are not whitespace.
- Length means the number of `char`s (Unicode scalar values), `word.chars().count()`, not the number of bytes: `"東京"` has 2 chars but 6 bytes.
- Look at the words of `a` first, in order, then the words of `b`. Return the first word with the largest char count; a later word must be strictly longer to replace it, so ties go to the earlier word, and so to `a`.
- If neither text has a word, return the empty view `&a[..0]`, which points at the start of `a`.

The result is always a slice of `a` or `b` itself; the function allocates nothing.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::longest_word("the quick fox", "a lazy dog")
Expected:   "quick"
"quick" has 5 characters; no other word is that long.

Expression: crate::longest_word("hi", "hello world")
Expected:   "hello"
"hello" and "world" tie at 5; the first one wins.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `a` and `b` are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes each and may be empty.
- No allocation in `longest_word` (`to_string`, `to_owned`, `String`, `format!`, `.clone()`, `to_vec`, `collect`). `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: Keep the best word so far and its length, starting from the empty view `&a[..0]` with length 0, and look at every word of `a` and then of `b`.

`text.split_whitespace()` yields `&str` slices of `text` itself, so they already have lifetime `'a`. Measure each with `chars().count()` and replace the best only when the new count is strictly greater.

`let mut best = &a[..0]; let mut best_count = 0; for text in [a, b] { for word in text.split_whitespace() { let count = word.chars().count(); if count > best_count { best = word; best_count = count; } } } best`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Start with `best = &a[..0]` and `best_count = 0`. Loop over the array `[a, b]` so `a` is scanned first, and over each text's `split_whitespace()` words. Replace `best` only for a strictly larger char count, which keeps the first longest word on ties. Every candidate is a slice of `a` or `b`, so `best` is a `&'a str` throughout and can be returned directly.
problems.idiomatic_md: `split_whitespace` gives borrowed slices, so finding a word never copies text, and one shared lifetime `'a` is the honest contract when the answer may come from either input. Counting `chars()` rather than `len()` is the right choice whenever a "length" is meant for people rather than for memory.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `a = text()` and `b = text()`. Call `crate::longest_word(&a, &b)` and compare with the oracle: split `a`, then `b`, at whitespace (space, tab, LF, U+3000), take the first word with the largest char count, or the empty slice at the start of `a` when there are no words. The result must be that exact slice (`std::ptr::eq`). Use the common generator, seed `0x0A00001F`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases answered from a 168; cases answered from b 132; cases where comparing byte lengths would pick another word 81; cases where a and b tie (a wins) 37.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Borrowed generic windows
problems.description_md:
A `Window<'a, T>` marks a range `start..end` of a borrowed slice. It is generic over the element type `T` and holds a reference, so it also has a lifetime parameter: a `Window` cannot outlive the slice it points into (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Struct Definitions"). Its fields are private, so `new` is the only way to make one, and `new` checks the range.

- `Window::new(items, start, end)` returns `Some(window)` when `start <= end` and `end <= items.len()`; otherwise it returns `None`. It must not panic for any `usize` values, including `usize::MAX`: compare before slicing, and never compute `end + 1` or similar.
- `view(&self) -> &[T]` returns `&items[start..end]`. Its output lifetime is elided, so by the third elision rule it borrows from `self` (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision"): the result can be used only while the `Window` is alive.
- `original(&self) -> &'a [T]` returns the same range, but with the lifetime `'a` of the underlying slice (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Method Definitions"). Its result may be kept after the `Window` is dropped, as long as the slice is alive.
- `kind(&self) -> &'static str` returns the literal `window`, which lives for the whole program (Book ch. 10.3, "The Static Lifetime").

None of the methods copies elements, so `T` needs no bounds; the tests use an element type with no traits.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let v = vec![10, 20, 30, 40]; match crate::Window::new(&v, 1, 3) { Some(w) => w.view().to_vec(), None => Vec::new() } }
Expected:   vec![20, 30]
Elements 1 and 2 of the vector are 20 and 30.

Expression: crate::Window::new(&[1, 2, 3], 2, 4).is_none()
Expected:   true
The slice has 3 elements, so the end 4 is out of range.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `items` holds up to 100,000 elements; `start` and `end` are any `usize` values.
- No bounds on `T`. No allocation (`to_vec`, `clone`, `collect`, `String`); `unwrap()` is banned. The struct stays as it is.
hints: `new` is the only place that needs logic: once it has checked the range, slicing in the other methods can never panic.
The two checks `start <= end` and `end <= items.len()` together imply `start <= items.len()`. `view` and `original` have the same body; only their signatures differ, and the signatures are supplied.
`new`: `if start <= end && end <= items.len() { Some(Self { items, start, end }) } else { None }`; `view` and `original`: `&self.items[self.start..self.end]`; `kind`: `"window"`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Validate the range in `new` with two comparisons and store it; return `None` otherwise. Both `view` and `original` slice `self.items` with the stored range. `self.items` is a `&'a [T]`, so slicing it gives a `&'a [T]`, which fits `original` exactly and can be shortened to the `&self` lifetime for `view`. `kind` returns a string literal.
problems.idiomatic_md: Checking invariants once in a constructor and keeping the fields private is how a type guarantees that its methods never panic. Choosing between an elided result (tied to `&self`) and an explicit `'a` result is a design decision: `'a` gives callers more freedom, so it is worth writing when the data really comes from the borrowed input.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` values, each `pick(100)`. Then draw `start`, then `end`; each is `usize::MAX` if `pick(8)` is 0, otherwise `pick(len + 3)`. Call `crate::Window::new(&v, start, end)` and compare with the oracle: `None` unless `start <= end <= len`; otherwise a window whose `view()` and `original()` are exactly `&v[start..end]` (`std::ptr::eq`) and whose `kind()` is `window`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000020`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases rejected because start > end 136; cases rejected because end > len 89; cases with a usize::MAX endpoint 75; cases with a valid non-empty window 58; cases with a valid empty window 17.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Understand a static type bound
problems.description_md:
`owned_static_label(value)` takes a value by value and returns its `Display` text, exactly as `format!("{}", value)` would. The interesting part is the bound, which is supplied:

```rust
pub fn owned_static_label<T: std::fmt::Display + 'static>(value: T) -> String
```

`T: 'static` does **not** mean "the value lives forever". It means the type `T` contains no references that could expire, so a value of that type could be kept as long as anyone likes (Book ch. 10.3, "The Static Lifetime"). Owned types qualify: `String`, `i32`, `char`, and your own structs without reference fields. A `String` passed in is moved into the function and dropped at its end, yet it meets the bound. A `&'static str` literal also qualifies. A reference to a local, such as `&String`, does not, because the reference would dangle once the local is gone; the compiler rejects such a call (one probe checks it).

- Return the value's `Display` output unchanged: no quotes, no padding, no trimming.
- `Display` is the only capability the body needs (Book ch. 10.2, "Trait Bound Syntax"); the tests use their own type that implements only `Display`.

Do not try to make a value "static" with `Box::leak` or by adding `'static` elsewhere; the point of the problem is to read the bound, not to fight it.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::owned_static_label(String::from("ready"))
Expected:   "ready".to_string()
A `String` owns its text, so it satisfies the bound.

Expression: crate::owned_static_label(42)
Expected:   "42".to_string()
Integers are `Display` and own no references.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Text values are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes.
- The signature stays as given. `Box::leak` and `unwrap()` are banned.
hints: The bound already says everything the function may do with `value`: display it.
`format!` with `{}` (or an inline `{value}`) calls the type's `Display` implementation and returns a `String`; `value.to_string()` does the same.
The whole body is `format!("{value}")`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Format the value with `format!("{value}")`. The `'static` bound changes nothing in the body; it only restricts which types callers may pass. Because `value` is owned by the function, it is dropped when the function returns, after its text has been copied into the new `String`.
problems.idiomatic_md: `T: 'static` appears on APIs that may keep a value indefinitely, such as `std::thread::spawn` (Chapter 16); it rules out borrowed data, not short-lived owned data. When the compiler asks for `'static`, the usual fix is to pass an owned value, not to make a borrow last longer.

For each case draw `k = pick(3)`: 0 draws `t = text()` and passes `String::from(t)`; 1 passes `next()` as a `u32`; 2 passes `next()` read as an `i32`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000021`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases passing a u32 109; cases passing an i32 101; cases passing an owned String 90; cases passing an empty String 1.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Generics, bounds and borrowed selection
problems.description_md:
This is the Book's closing example of Chapter 10 with a twist (Book ch. 10.3, "Generic Type Parameters, Trait Bounds, and Lifetimes Together"). `announced_choice(a, b, announcement)` chooses one of two texts and also builds an announcement message:

```rust
pub fn announced_choice<'a, T: std::fmt::Display>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str, announcement: T) -> (&'a str, String)
```

- The chosen text is the one with **more chars** (`chars().count()`, Unicode scalar values, not bytes). If both have the same count, choose `a`. Return the input itself, not a copy.
- The message is `Choosing: ` followed by the announcement's `Display` text, as an owned `String`.

The signature combines all three ideas of the chapter: a lifetime `'a` ties the chosen text to both inputs, a generic `T` lets the announcement be any type, and the bound `T: Display` is the one capability the body needs. The announcement is taken by value and its text copied into the new `String`, so the returned pair does not borrow from it: the caller may pass a reference to a short-lived value and keep using the chosen text after that value is gone. The tests use an announcement type with only `Display`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::announced_choice("apple", "fig", 3)
Expected:   ("apple", "Choosing: 3".to_string())
"apple" has 5 chars, "fig" 3.

Expression: crate::announced_choice("hi", "hello", "today")
Expected:   ("hello", "Choosing: today".to_string())
"hello" is longer than "hi".
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `a` and `b` are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes and may be empty.
- The signature stays as given. Do not copy the chosen text (`to_string`, `to_owned`, `.clone()` on `a` or `b`); `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: There are two independent results: a choice between `a` and `b`, and a message built from the announcement.
Compare `a.chars().count()` with `b.chars().count()` using `>=`, so a tie keeps `a`; the message is one `format!` call that uses the announcement's `Display`.
`let chosen = if a.chars().count() >= b.chars().count() { a } else { b }; (chosen, format!("Choosing: {announcement}"))`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Count the chars of both texts and pick `a` when its count is at least `b`'s, otherwise `b`; both are `&'a str`, so either can be returned as is. Build the message with `format!("Choosing: {announcement}")`, which uses `T: Display` and produces an owned `String` that does not borrow from `announcement`.
problems.idiomatic_md: Keeping the borrowed result (`&'a str`) and the owned result (`String`) separate in the return type makes the lifetimes obvious: only the first is tied to the inputs. A generic parameter with a `Display` bound accepts numbers, strings and caller-defined types alike.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `a = text()`, `b = text()` and `announcement = next()` as a `u32`. problems.title: Stable generic borrowed merge
problems.description_md:
`merge(a, b)` combines two slices that are each already sorted in non-decreasing order into one sorted list of references. It is the merge step of merge sort, written generically (Book ch. 10.1, "In Function Definitions") with the single bound it needs, `T: PartialOrd` for `<=` (Book ch. 10.2, "Trait Bound Syntax"), and a lifetime `'a` shared by both inputs and the output (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Function Signatures"):

```rust
pub fn merge<'a, T: PartialOrd>(a: &'a [T], b: &'a [T]) -> Vec<&'a T>
```

- Keep one position in each slice. While both have elements left, compare the current elements: if `a`'s is **less than or equal to** `b`'s, take a reference to `a`'s and advance in `a`; otherwise take `b`'s and advance in `b`.
- When one slice runs out, append references to everything left in the other.
- Every element of both inputs appears exactly once; duplicates are kept. When elements are equal, the one from `a` comes first, which makes the merge *stable*.

The output holds references into the inputs, so nothing is copied, cloned or sorted again, and the elements need no `Clone` or `Ord`. You may assume both inputs are sorted and contain no `NaN`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::merge(&[1, 4, 9], &[2, 3, 10])
Expected:   vec![&1, &2, &3, &4, &9, &10]
Elements are taken from whichever slice has the smaller next value.

Expression: crate::merge::<i32>(&[], &[])
Expected:   Vec::<&i32>::new()
Nothing to merge.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Each input holds up to 100,000 elements and is sorted in non-decreasing order.
- The bound is exactly `T: PartialOrd`. `sort`, `.clone()`, `concat`, `extend` and `unwrap()` are banned.
hints: Use two indices, one per slice, and a `while` loop that runs while both still have elements; afterwards, one of the slices may still have a tail.
Compare `a[i] <= b[j]` (two `T` values, compared through `PartialOrd`, nothing moved) and push `&a[i]` or `&b[j]`. Using `<=` rather than `<` is what puts equal elements from `a` first.
Main loop: `if a[i] <= b[j] { out.push(&a[i]); i += 1; } else { out.push(&b[j]); j += 1; }`; then two more `while` loops push the rest of `a` from `i` and the rest of `b` from `j`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Walk both slices with indices `i` and `j`. Each step pushes the smaller current element, preferring `a` on ties, and advances that index; each element is visited once, so the work is proportional to the total length. When one index reaches the end, the remaining elements of the other slice are already in order, so they are pushed as they are.
problems.idiomatic_md: A merge that returns references keeps the elements where they are, so it works for any `PartialOrd` type and costs only one pointer per element. Breaking ties in favour of the left input is the property that lets merge sort keep equal elements in their original order.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `la = pick(13)` and `la` values, each `pick(9) - 4`, then `lb = pick(13)` and `lb` values the same way; sort each list. Call `crate::merge(&a, &b)` and compare with the oracle, a standard two-index merge that takes from `a` when `a[i] <= b[j]`: the result must have length `la + lb` and its `k`-th reference must point at the oracle's `k`-th element (`std::ptr::eq`). Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000023`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with equal values in both inputs 223; cases where a runs out first 172; cases where b runs out first 78; cases with an empty side 50.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Generic result ledger
problems.description_md:
A `Ledger<T, E>` records the outcomes of a series of operations in the order they happen. It is a generic struct holding a vector of a generic enum (Book ch. 10.1, "In Struct Definitions" and "In Enum Definitions"), and its methods are split over two `impl` blocks with different bounds (Book ch. 10.2, "Using Trait Bounds to Conditionally Implement Methods"). The types and the empty `new` are supplied.

In `impl<T, E> Ledger<T, E>`, with **no bounds**, so every ledger has these methods:

- `value(&mut self, value)`, `error(&mut self, error)` and `empty(&mut self)` append `Outcome::Value(value)`, `Outcome::Error(error)` and `Outcome::Empty` to `entries`.
- `into_parts(self)` consumes the ledger and returns `(values, errors, empty_count)`: every `Value` payload in recording order, every `Error` payload in recording order, and the number of `Empty` entries. The payloads are moved out, not copied.

In `impl<T: Display, E: Display> Ledger<T, E>`, so only ledgers whose payloads can be displayed have it:

- `report(&self)` returns one line per entry, in recording order: `value:{v}` for a value, `error:{e}` for an error and `empty` for an empty entry, joined with `\n`, with no line feed after the last line. A ledger with no entries reports an empty string. Payload text is written as `Display` writes it; a payload that contains a line feed keeps it.

`report` borrows the ledger, so it can be called any number of times before `into_parts`. The tests record payloads with no traits at all, which must still work for recording and `into_parts`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let mut ledger = crate::Ledger::new(); ledger.value(5); ledger.error(String::from("bad")); ledger.empty(); ledger.report() }
Expected:   "value:5\nerror:bad\nempty".to_string()
Three entries give three lines, with no line feed at the end.

Expression: { let mut ledger = crate::Ledger::new(); ledger.value("a"); ledger.error(7u8); ledger.value("b"); ledger.empty(); ledger.into_parts() }
Expected:   (vec!["a", "b"], vec![7], 1)
Values "a" and "b", error 7, one empty entry.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 100,000 entries with at most 100,000 bytes of payload text.
- Keep the two `impl` blocks and their bounds as supplied. `.clone()` and `unwrap()` are banned.
hints: The three recording methods are one `push` each. `into_parts` and `report` both walk `entries` with a `match`; the difference is whether they own the entries or only borrow them.

`into_parts` takes `self`, so `for entry in self.entries` gives owned outcomes whose payloads can be moved into two vectors. `report` takes `&self`, so loop over `&self.entries` and format each payload through `Display`; collect the lines in a `Vec<String>` and `join("\n")` them.

Recording: `self.entries.push(Outcome::Value(value))` and so on. In `report`: `match entry { Outcome::Value(value) => lines.push(format!("value:{value}")), Outcome::Error(error) => lines.push(format!("error:{error}")), Outcome::Empty => lines.push(String::from("empty")) }`, then `lines.join("\n")`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Recording pushes the matching variant. `into_parts` consumes the vector with a by-value loop and a `match`, moving each payload into its list and counting `Empty`. `report` loops over references to the entries, formats each as one line and joins the lines with `\n`, which adds separators only between lines and gives an empty string for an empty ledger. The `Display` bound is needed only for `format!`, so it sits on `report`'s `impl` alone.
problems.idiomatic_md: Splitting `impl` blocks by bound keeps a generic type as widely usable as possible: any payloads can be recorded and taken apart, and only the operation that needs `Display` asks for it. Pairing a borrowing method (`report`) with a consuming one (`into_parts`) is how a collection offers both a view and a hand-off without cloning.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `count = pick(25)`, then `count` operations on a new `Ledger<String, u32>`. For each operation draw `op = pick(3)`: 0 records `value(text())`; 1 records `error(next())`; 2 records `empty()`. Then call `report()` followed by `into_parts()` and compare both with the oracle: the report has one line per operation (`value:{text}`, `error:{n}` or `empty`) joined with `\n`, and the parts are the texts in order, the numbers in order and the count of empty entries. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000024`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with a value containing a line feed 243; cases recording all three kinds 236; cases recording one or two kinds 53; cases with no entries 11.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Ordered record index
problems.description_md:
A `Record` pairs a numeric `id` with a text `label`. Its comparison traits are derived, and a derived ordering compares fields in the order they are declared: first `id` numerically, then `label` (Book ch. 10.2, "Implementing a Trait on a Type"; L10.5 covers derived ordering). Labels compare by their UTF-8 bytes, so `"Z" < "a" < "é"`; there is no locale-aware collation. Implement two standard traits and one function:

- `impl std::fmt::Display for Record`: the id in decimal, a colon, and the label exactly, such as `7:seven`. An empty label gives `7:`; a label may itself contain `:`.
- `impl From<(u32, String)> for Record`: `Record::from((7, String::from("seven")))` builds the record from the tuple, moving the `String` in. `From` also makes `(7, String::from("seven")).into()` work.
- `record_index(records)` takes ownership of a vector of records, sorts it, removes records that are **identical** (same id and same label), and returns the `Display` text of each remaining record, in sorted order. Records with the same id but different labels are all kept.

After sorting, identical records sit next to each other, so the standard `dedup()` (Chapter 8) removes exactly the duplicates. Sort the records themselves, not their texts: `10:x` must come after `9:x`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::record_index(vec![crate::Record::from((2, String::from("b"))), crate::Record::from((1, String::from("z"))), crate::Record::from((2, String::from("a")))])
Expected:   vec!["1:z".to_string(), "2:a".to_string(), "2:b".to_string()]
Id 1 comes first; the two id-2 records are ordered by label.

Expression: crate::Record::from((7, String::from("seven"))).to_string()
Expected:   "7:seven".to_string()
The id, a colon, then the label.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 100,000 records; ids are any `u32`, labels valid UTF-8.
- The struct and its derives stay as they are. `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: The derived `Ord` already defines the order you need; your work is formatting, converting, and using the derives in the right order.

`fmt` writes with `write!(f, ...)`; `from` takes the tuple apart with `value.0` and `value.1`. In `record_index`, mark the parameter `mut records`, then `sort()` and `dedup()` before formatting anything.
`write!(f, "{}:{}", self.id, self.label)`; `Self { id: value.0, label: value.1 }`; `records.sort(); records.dedup();` then push `record.to_string()` for each record.
problems.solution_approach_md: `Display::fmt` writes `id:label`. `From::from` moves the two tuple fields into a `Record`. `record_index` owns its vector, so it can sort it in place with the derived `Ord` (id first, then label bytes) and call `dedup()`, which removes consecutive equal records; after sorting, all identical records are consecutive. Each remaining record is formatted with `to_string()`, which `Display` provides.
problems.idiomatic_md: Deriving `Ord` on a struct whose fields are in priority order gives a correct multi-key sort for free, and `sort` + `dedup` is the standard way to get the unique values of an `Ord` vector without a set. Formatting last keeps the comparison on typed values.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `len = pick(25)`, then `len` records. For each record draw `id = pick(6)`, then `k = pick(3)` for the label: 0 gives `text()`; 1 gives one of `["a", "b", "é"]` chosen with `pick(3)`; 2 gives the empty string. Call `crate::record_index` on the records built with `Record::from` and compare with the oracle: the distinct `(id, label)` pairs sorted by id and then by label bytes, each written `id:label`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000025`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases keeping different labels for one ID 258; cases with identical records removed 202; cases with no records 9.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Borrowed opaque reports
problems.description_md:
This problem combines a trait with a default method, a struct that holds a reference, and an opaque return type. The trait `View` has two required methods and a default `describe` that joins them with ` / ` (Book ch. 10.2, "Default Implementations"). `Report<'a>` stores a borrowed `selected` text and an owned `message` (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Struct Definitions"); it and its `impl View` are supplied. Write two functions:

- `borrowed_report(a, b, announcement)` returns a `Report` whose `selected` is the text with **more bytes** (`len()`), `a` on a tie, and whose `message` is `Selected: ` followed by the announcement's `Display` text. The selected text is `a` or `b` itself, not a copy.
- `describe(view)` takes any `&impl View` and returns `view.describe()`, so a type that overrides `describe` is described its own way (Book ch. 10.2, "Traits as Parameters").

The return type of `borrowed_report` is `impl View + use<'a, T>` (Book ch. 10.2, "Returning Types That Implement Traits"). In edition 2024 an `impl Trait` return captures every lifetime and type parameter in scope unless a `use<...>` list says otherwise (L10.5 introduces `use<>`). Here the list names `'a`, because the report really borrows `a` or `b`, and `T`, the announcement type; it leaves out the anonymous lifetime of the `&T` reference. That is a promise that the report does not borrow the announcement, which holds because its text is copied into the owned `message`. So the caller may drop the announcement right after the call, but must keep `a` and `b` alive while using the report. The caller sees only `impl View`: `Report`'s fields stay hidden.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::describe(&crate::borrowed_report("apple", "fig", &3))
Expected:   "apple / Selected: 3".to_string()
"apple" has 5 bytes, "fig" 3.

Expression: crate::describe(&crate::borrowed_report("fig", "banana", &"fruit"))
Expected:   "banana / Selected: fruit".to_string()
"banana" is longer than "fig".
```
problems.constraints_md:
- `a` and `b` are valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes and may be empty.
- The signatures stay as given. Do not copy `a` or `b` (`to_string`, `to_owned`, `.clone()` in `borrowed_report`); `unwrap()` is banned.
hints: `borrowed_report` makes two decisions, which text to borrow and what message to own; `describe` makes none: it asks the view.

Compare `a.len()` with `b.len()` (bytes) using `>=` and store the chosen `&'a str` in the `Report`. Build the message with `format!`, which copies the announcement's text so the report does not borrow it.
`let selected = if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }; Report { selected, message: format!("Selected: {announcement}") }`; `describe` is `view.describe()`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Choose `a` when its byte length is at least `b`'s, otherwise `b`; both are `&'a str`, which is what `Report<'a>` stores. Format the message from the announcement into a new `String`. The value returned is a `Report<'a>`, which mentions only `'a`, so it fits the promise `use<'a, T>`. `describe` forwards to the trait method, which runs the default or an override.
problems.idiomatic_md: A precise `use<...>` list documents exactly what a returned `impl Trait` may borrow, which matters most when a function takes several references with different roles. Forwarding to a trait method (`view.describe()`) instead of re-implementing it keeps customised implementors working.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `a = text()`, `b = text()` and `announcement = next()` as a `u32`. Create the announcement in an inner block, call `crate::borrowed_report(&a, &b, &announcement)`, and let the block end. Then compare with the oracle: `selected()` is `a` if `a.len() >= b.len()` in bytes, otherwise `b` (checked with `std::ptr::eq`), and `crate::describe(&view)` is that text, ` / Selected: ` and the number in decimal. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000026`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases selecting b 153; cases selecting a (more bytes) 144; cases where comparing character counts would select the other text 27; cases with equal byte lengths (a wins) 3.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Borrowed document index
problems.description_md:
A `Document<'a>` indexes the words of a borrowed text once, so later lookups do not need to split the text again. It stores the text and a `Vec<&'a str>` of word views, all pointing into the same text, so a `Document` cannot outlive that text (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Struct Definitions"). Its methods show the lifetime choices a method can make (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision", "Lifetime Annotations in Method Definitions" and "The Static Lifetime"):

- `new(text)` splits `text` with `split_whitespace()` (Unicode whitespace: space, tab, line feed, U+3000, …) and stores every word, in order. This is the only place the text is split.
- `first(&self) -> Option<&str>`: the first word, or `None`. The output lifetime is elided, so it borrows from the `Document` and may be used only while the `Document` is alive.
- `at(&self, index) -> Option<&'a str>`: the word at `index` (counting from 0), or `None` if there is none, for any `usize` including `usize::MAX`, without panicking. Its result has the text's lifetime `'a`, so it may be kept after the `Document` is dropped.
- `words(&self) -> &[&'a str]`: all words, as a slice of the stored vector.
- `text(&self) -> &'a str`: the whole original text, unchanged.
- `label(&self) -> &'static str`: the literal `document`.

Every returned word is a view into the original text; nothing is copied.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let d = crate::Document::new("the quick  fox"); (d.first(), d.at(2), d.words().len()) }
Expected:   (Some("the"), Some("fox"), 3)
Two spaces still separate just two words.

Expression: { let d = crate::Document::new(""); (d.first(), d.at(0), d.words().len(), d.text(), d.label()) }
Expected:   (None, None, 0, "", "document")
Nothing to index, so every lookup is `None`.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- The text is valid UTF-8 of up to 100,000 bytes and has at most 100,000 words.
- No allocation of text (`to_string`, `to_owned`, `String`, `format!`, `.clone()`, `collect`); `unwrap()` is banned. Only `new` may call `split_whitespace`.
hints: Do all the splitting in `new`; every other method reads a field.

`split_whitespace()` yields `&'a str` views of `text`, so they can be pushed into `Vec<&'a str>` as they are. For lookups, `self.words.get(index)` returns `Option<&&'a str>` without panicking, and `.copied()` (Chapter 8) turns it into `Option<&'a str>`.

`new`: push every `word` of `text.split_whitespace()` into `words`, then `Self { text, words }`. `first`: `self.words.first().copied()`; `at`: `self.words.get(index).copied()`; `text`: `self.text`; `label`: `"document"`.
problems.solution_approach_md: `new` builds the word list once. The lookups use the vector's `first` and `get`, which return `None` instead of panicking for a missing index, and `copied()` turns the `&&str` they give into the stored `&'a str`. `at` and `text` return `&'a str` values taken from the fields, so their results live as long as the text; `first` returns the same kind of value but its elided signature shortens it to the `Document`'s borrow.
problems.idiomatic_md: Precomputing borrowed views is cheap: the index is a vector of (pointer, length) pairs, and no text is copied. Writing `'a` on `at` and `text` but eliding it on `first` is a deliberate API choice; the stronger signature gives callers more freedom, and the compiler enforces whichever you choose.

Compare with the oracle: the word at that position as the same slice of `s` (`std::ptr::eq`), or `None` past the end, and the number of words. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000027`, exactly 300 cases.
