problems.title: Generic borrowed query engine
problems.description_md:
`query` searches a slice of items for those whose text matches a query, and returns both the matching items and a printable report. It brings together the whole chapter (Book ch. 10.3, "Generic Type Parameters, Trait Bounds, and Lifetimes Together"):

```rust
pub fn query<'a, T>(items: &'a [T], query: &str, announcement: &impl std::fmt::Display) -> (Vec<&'a T>, String)
where
    T: Textual + std::fmt::Display,
```

The trait `Textual` gives access to an item's text; `Entry<T>` implements it for every `T`, and implements `Display` as `key:text` only when its key is `Display` (a conditional implementation, Book ch. 10.2, "Using Trait Bounds to Conditionally Implement Methods"). These are supplied. The `where` clause asks for exactly the two capabilities the body uses (Book ch. 10.2, "Clearer Trait Bounds with `where` Clauses").

- Lower-case the query with `to_lowercase()` and split it with `split_whitespace()` into query words. Lower-case each item's `text()` the same way.
- An item **matches** when every query word occurs somewhere in its lower-cased text, as a substring (`contains`), in any order. A query with no words (empty or whitespace only) matches every item.
- Return the matching items as references into `items`, in their original order, and a report: the announcement's `Display` text, a line feed, then the `Display` text of each matching item, joined with line feeds. With no matches the report is the announcement followed by one line feed.

Lower-casing is whole-string Unicode lower-casing (`"É"` becomes `"é"`); there is no other normalisation, so `"é"` does not match `"e\u{301}"`. The returned references have lifetime `'a` and borrow only `items`: the query string and the announcement may be dropped right after the call.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let items = vec![crate::Entry { key: 1, text: String::from("Rust book") }, crate::Entry { key: 2, text: String::from("Go guide") }, crate::Entry { key: 3, text: String::from("rust NOTES") }]; let (found, report) = crate::query(&items, "rust", &"Found:"); (found.len(), found[0].key, found[1].key, report) }
Expected:   (2, 1, 3, "Found:\n1:Rust book\n3:rust NOTES".to_string())
Entries 1 and 3 contain "rust" in some case.

Expression: { let items = vec![crate::Entry { key: 1, text: String::from("a") }, crate::Entry { key: 2, text: String::new() }]; let (found, report) = crate::query(&items, "", &"All:"); (found.len(), report) }
Expected:   (2, "All:\n1:a\n2:".to_string())
No query words means nothing can be missing.
```
problems.constraints_md:
- Up to 500 items with at most 50,000 bytes of text in total; the query is at most 256 bytes.
- The signature and the supplied items stay as they are. `.clone()` and `unwrap()` are banned.
hints: Lower-case the query once, before the loop. For each item, decide whether it matches, and if it does, remember the reference and its report line.

A match test is a loop over the query's words with a flag that turns false at the first word the item's lower-cased text does not `contains`; with no words, the flag stays true. `item.text()` comes from `Textual`, and `item.to_string()` from `Display`.

In the loop: `let text = item.text().to_lowercase(); let mut matches = true; for word in wanted.split_whitespace() { if !text.contains(word) { matches = false; break; } } if matches { found.push(item); lines.push(item.to_string()); }`; return `(found, format!("{}\n{}", announcement, lines.join("\n")))`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Lower-case the query once. For each item, lower-case its text and check every query word with `contains`; the item matches if none is missing, which is automatically true for a query without words. Push matching items (each `item` is already a `&'a T`) and their `Display` lines. Build the report with `format!`, putting the announcement and a line feed before the joined lines. The result borrows only `items`, as the signature says.
problems.idiomatic_md: A `where` clause keeps a signature with several bounds readable, and asking only for `Textual + Display` means any type that can show its text works, not just `Entry`. Returning references instead of cloned items keeps the search cheap and lets the caller act on the original items.
problems.random_md:
For each case draw `n = pick(4)` entries with keys `1..=n`. For each entry draw `k = pick(3)` for its text: 0 gives `text()`; 1 gives `Rust é東`; 2 gives `a z`. Then draw the query with `pick(7)` from `["", "a", "é", "東", "rust", "A Z", "Z\u{3000}a"]` and the announcement `Q` followed by the digit `pick(10)`. Call `crate::query(&items, query, &announcement)` and compare with the oracle: an entry matches when every whitespace-separated word of the lower-cased query occurs in its lower-cased text; the result must reference the matching entries in order (`std::ptr::eq`), and the report is the announcement, `\n`, and the matching entries' `key:text` lines joined with `\n`. Use the common generator, seed `0x0A000028`, exactly 300 cases.

Realized coverage over the 300 cases: cases with no entries 94; cases matching every entry 84; cases matching some entries 64; cases matching no entry 58; cases whose query has no words (all match) 47.

The generated cases are run against the compiled reference solution, and the oracle above computes every expected result independently.

problems.title: Generic leaderboard
problems.description_md:
A game keeps a leaderboard: players join, and the board can list them from best to worst, name the leader, show the top few and print a report. This project writes that board once, for any kind of entry, using the three tools of Chapter 10: a generic struct that stores the entries (Book ch. 10.1, "Generic Data Types"), a trait that says what an entry must be able to answer before it can be ranked (Book ch. 10.2, "Traits: Defining Shared Behavior"), and a struct of references with a lifetime parameter for a view of the ranking (Book ch. 10.3, "Validating References with Lifetimes"). You edit one file, `src/lib.rs`. Runtime rows include it as a module, glob-import it at the harness crate root and call it as `crate::Leaderboard::new()`, `crate::Player { … }` and so on; the trait `Ranked` is then in scope for method calls. Many rows rank a type of their own, such as `struct Team { name: &'static str, score: i64 }` with only `impl crate::Ranked for Team`, so the board must work with exactly what the trait promises.

The starter gives every signature, the struct definitions and the `Player` type with its `impl Ranked`. Keep them as they are: the trait `Ranked` with the methods `points(&self) -> i64`, `label(&self) -> &str` and `summary(&self) -> String`; `Player` with public fields `name: String` and `points: i64`; `Leaderboard<T>` with one private field `entries: Vec<T>`; and `RankingView<'a, T>` with one public field `entries: Vec<&'a T>`.

**Part 1 · A trait and a generic board**

`Ranked` has two required methods, `points` and `label`, and one default method, `summary`, whose body you write in the trait itself (Book ch. 10.2, "Default Implementations"). The default returns the label, a colon, a space and the points in decimal, `format!("{}: {}", self.label(), self.points())`, for example `Ada: 42` or `low: -9223372036854775808`. It calls the two required methods, so every implementor gets it, `Player` and the test types alike, and an implementor may still override it. The label is used exactly as the implementor returns it: no trimming, and an empty label, a line feed or a NUL stays in the text.

`Leaderboard<T>` owns its entries. Its first three methods are in an `impl<T> Leaderboard<T>` block with no bounds (Book ch. 10.1, "In Method Definitions"), because storing and counting need nothing from `T`: `new()` returns an empty board, `add(entry)` moves the entry onto the end of `entries`, and `len()` returns how many entries were added. A board of a type that implements no trait at all can be created, filled and counted.

**Part 2 · Ranking with a trait bound**

The ranking methods need `points`, so they go in a second block, `impl<T: Ranked> Leaderboard<T>`; they exist only for boards whose entries are `Ranked` (Book ch. 10.2, "Using Trait Bounds to Conditionally Implement Methods"). Their signatures take `&self` and return references without naming a lifetime: by the third elision rule, the references borrow the board (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision").

`ranking()` returns a `Vec<&T>` with a reference to every stored entry, highest `points()` first. Entries with equal points keep the order in which they were added, so the ranking is stable. The board itself is not reordered, and nothing is copied: every reference points into `entries`. Compare scores directly with `>` or `<`; negating or subtracting them overflows at `i64::MIN` and `i64::MAX`. Without closures there is no `sort_by` (Chapter 13). A short loop does the job: push a reference to each entry, then move each new reference to the left while its points are strictly greater than its left neighbour's; stopping at an equal neighbour is what keeps ties in insertion order. (Sorting keys with `sort()`, such as pairs of a score and an insertion index, is also allowed if the order is the same.)

`best()` returns `Some` reference to the entry with the highest points, the earliest one when several share it, or `None` for an empty board. It finds the answer in one pass over `entries`, replacing the current best only when an entry has strictly more points.

**Part 3 · Borrowed views**

`top(limit)` returns the first `limit` references of the ranking: none for 0, and every entry when `limit` is at least the number of entries, `usize::MAX` included, so the limit must not be increased or used in arithmetic that can overflow. `Vec::truncate` does exactly this.

A `RankingView<'a, T>` is a value that holds references, so its definition names their lifetime: a view cannot outlive the board its references point into (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Struct Definitions"). `view(limit)` returns `RankingView { entries: self.top(limit) }`; its return type `RankingView<'_, T>` says that the view borrows from `self`.

`RankingView::first()` returns the view's first reference, or `None` when the view is empty. It lives in an `impl<'a, T> RankingView<'a, T>` block with no bounds, and its return type is `Option<&'a T>`, written out rather than elided (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Method Definitions"). With elision the result would borrow the view itself, `&self`, and could not be used once the view is dropped; with `'a` it borrows only the board, so a caller may keep the leader after throwing the view away. A view that a caller builds directly, `RankingView { entries: vec![&a, &b] }`, is taken as given: `first` returns its first reference, with no check that the entries are ranked.

**Part 4 · Reports**

`RankingView::summary()` is in an `impl<'a, T: Ranked> RankingView<'a, T>` block. It calls each entry's own `summary()`, so a type that overrides `summary` is reported with its own text, and joins the lines with LF and no final LF; an empty view gives the empty string. `Leaderboard::report()` is the summary of a view of every entry, `self.view(usize::MAX).summary()`: the whole ranking, one line per entry, best first.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Setup: let mut b = crate::Leaderboard::new(); b.add(crate::Player { name: "rust".to_string(), points: 7 }); b.add(crate::Player { name: "other".to_string(), points: 3 });
Expression: b.report()
Expected: "rust: 7\nother: 3".to_string()
```

```text
Setup: struct Team { name: &'static str, score: i64 } impl crate::Ranked for Team { fn points(&self) -> i64 { self.score } fn label(&self) -> &str { self.name } } let mut b = crate::Leaderboard::new(); b.add(Team { name: "A", score: 5 }); b.add(Team { name: "B", score: 9 }); b.add(Team { name: "C", score: 5 });
Expression: (b.len(), b.top(2).len(), b.report())
Expected: (3, 2, "B: 9\nA: 5\nC: 5".to_string())
```

```text
Setup: (the board above)
Expression: { let first; { let view = b.view(1); first = view.first(); } match first { Some(t) => t.label().to_string(), None => String::new() } }
Expected: "B".to_string()
```
problems.constraints_md:
- At most 2,000 entries per board; labels are valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes in total. Points use the full `i64` range; limits the full `usize` range.
- Keep every signature, struct field and visibility of the starter. `entries` stays private; `new`, `add` and `len` stay in an `impl<T>` block without bounds.
- No bound anywhere names `Clone` or `Copy`, and no entry is cloned: every result is a reference to a stored entry.
- Chapters 1–10 only: no `unwrap()`, no closures or closure-taking methods, no `dyn`, no `unsafe`.
hints: Put `new`, `add` and `len` in `impl<T> Leaderboard<T>` and everything that calls `points()` in `impl<T: Ranked> Leaderboard<T>`; the default `summary` belongs inside `trait Ranked { … }`, not in `impl Ranked for Player`.

For `ranking`, start with `let mut out: Vec<&T> = Vec::new(); for entry in &self.entries { out.push(entry); }`, then for each index `i` from 1 move `out[j]` left with `out.swap(j, j - 1)` while `j > 0 && out[j].points() > out[j - 1].points()`. `best` keeps an `Option<&T>` and replaces it only on a strictly greater score.

`top` is `let mut out = self.ranking(); out.truncate(limit); out`. `first` is `if self.entries.is_empty() { None } else { Some(self.entries[0]) }` with the return type `Option<&'a T>`. `summary` pushes `'\n'` before every entry except the first, then `entry.summary()`; `report` is `self.view(usize::MAX).summary()`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Storage and ranking are separate `impl` blocks: the unbounded one owns and counts entries of any type, and the `T: Ranked` one is the only code that looks at scores. `ranking` builds a vector of references and orders it with a stable insertion sort that compares `points()` directly; `best` is a single pass that keeps the first strict maximum; `top` truncates the ranking, and `view` wraps it. `RankingView` stores references with the board's lifetime `'a`, which `first` returns unchanged, so the result outlives the view. `summary` asks each entry for its own `summary()` and joins the lines, and `report` is the summary of the full view.
problems.idiomatic_md: Putting each method in the least-constrained `impl` block that can hold it keeps the type useful: a board of anything can be stored and counted, and only ranking demands `Ranked`, so a caller never has to implement a trait it does not need. Returning references instead of copies means no entry type has to be `Clone`, and naming `'a` in `first` documents exactly what the result borrows: the board, not the temporary view.
problems.random_md:
Row 32. Reset the generator to seed `0x0A000101` once and generate 300 boards. For each, draw n = pick(9) (0 to 8 entries). For entry number `id` = 0, 1, …, n − 1 draw kind = pick(5): kind 0 gives points `i64::MIN`, kind 1 `i64::MAX`, kinds 2 and 3 give pick(5) − 2 (−2 to 2, so ties are common), and kind 4 gives next() − 2147483648; then draw the label with text(). Each entry is a test type `Entry { id: usize, name: String, score: i64 }` that implements only `Ranked` (`points` is `score`, `label` is `name`) and is added to a new board. Finally draw lk = pick(4): the limit is 0 for lk = 0, 1 + pick(n + 1) for lk = 1, n for lk = 2 and `usize::MAX` for lk = 3.

The oracle orders the ids by repeatedly taking the remaining entry with the highest score, the smallest id among equals. Each case compares, by `id` (that is, by entry identity): `best()`, `top(limit)`, `view(limit).first()`, and the exact texts `view(limit).summary()` and `report()`, built from `label: points` lines joined by LF, plus `len()`. Realized over the 300 boards: board sizes 0 to 8 occur 45, 31, 30, 38, 32, 33, 31, 30 and 30 times; the 1,134 entries have points `i64::MIN` 227 times, `i64::MAX` 246, a small value 419 and a wide value 242; 136 boards contain a tie, 71 of them a tie for the highest score; limit kinds 0 to 3 occur 65, 78, 77 and 80 times; and in 101 boards the view is shorter than the board. The reference solution and the oracle agree on all 300 boards.
problems.source_checks_md:
- Required: `Leaderboard<T>` has exactly one field, the private `entries: Vec<T>`; `new`, `add` and `len` are in an `impl<T> Leaderboard<T>` block with no bounds; `ranking`, `best`, `top`, `view` and `report` are in a block whose only bound is `T: Ranked`; `RankingView::first` is in an `impl` without bounds; and no bound anywhere names `Clone` or `Copy`.
- Required: no closure expression (`|…|`) and no call to `sort_by`, `sort_by_key`, `map`, `filter`, `collect`, `max_by_key`, `retain` or `clone` anywhere in the learner file; no `unwrap()`, no `dyn` and no `unsafe`.
problems.notes_md:
Starter: compiles with warnings (the unused variables `entry` and `limit`, and `entries` never read) and fails every runtime row except 3, 14 and 22, whose empty boards the placeholders already answer correctly; it also fails the suite (row 32). It passes the compiler probes 33–36 and the source rules 37 and 38, which concern the signatures and bounds it already has. The Part-N checkpoint is the reference with the methods of later Parts still the starter's placeholders: measured, the Part 1 checkpoint passes rows 1–8, the Part 2 checkpoint rows 1–16 and the Part 3 checkpoint rows 1–23, and the reference passes every row and the suite. Measured with wrong versions of the reference: letting an entry pass an equal score in the insertion loop (`>=`) fails rows 11, 16 and 23 and 136 suite boards; keeping the last of tied leaders in `best` fails rows 12 and 23; ranking lowest first fails 14 rows; comparing negated scores panics with an overflow in rows 13 and 29; a final LF after the last line fails rows 24–31; building each line from `label` and `points` instead of calling `summary` fails row 27; eliding the lifetime in `first` (`Option<&T>`) makes row 20 fail to compile; requiring `T: Ranked` for `new`, `add` and `len` fails rows 4 and 34 and rule 37; keeping one entry too many in `top` fails rows 17–19, 25 and 26; another default format (`label - points`) fails rows 1, 5–8, 24–26 and 28–31; a view that ignores its limit fails rows 19, 25 and 26; and returning the last entry from `first` fails rows 19 and 21. Row 31 is the `large` row: 2,000 entries added in rising order, the worst case for the insertion sort, take about 0.07 seconds in a debug build. A board holds at most 2,000 entries because the insertion sort that Part 2 teaches takes time proportional to the square of the board size. Rows 4 and 21 store types that implement no trait at all, and every row that defines `Team` or `Loud` gives it only `impl crate::Ranked`.

problems.title: Search with a trait
problems.description_md:
LM9's catalogue can look up books by title (`search_titles`), and nothing else. LM10 adds a trait for "something a query can be matched against", implements it for books and members, and writes one generic `search` function that works for both, and for any type a later chapter adds (Book ch. 10.2, "Traits: Defining Shared Behavior"). It also gives `Book` a `Display` implementation and the catalogue two new queries that return borrowed results. Runtime rows run in a harness whose crate root is the learner's `src/lib.rs`, so they name the root re-exports as `crate::Book`, `crate::Library`, `crate::search` and so on, and the trait `Searchable` is in scope for method calls through its re-export. Several rows implement `Searchable` for a type of their own that has no derives at all.

**Part 1 · The `Searchable` trait**

The starter is the accepted LM9 reference solution, file for file and unchanged. Add a file `src/search.rs`, declare it in `src/lib.rs` with `pub mod search;`, and re-export the trait with `pub use search::Searchable;` (Part 2 extends this line to `pub use search::{Searchable, search};`).

`Searchable` has one required method and one default method (Book ch. 10.2, "Defining a Trait" and "Default Implementations"):

- `fn search_text(&self) -> String;` the text a query is matched against;
- `fn matches(&self, query: &str) -> bool`, with a default body in the trait: lowercase the whole search text with `to_lowercase`, lowercase the whole query the same way, split the lowercased query into words with `split_whitespace`, and answer `true` exactly when every word is contained in the lowercased text (`str::contains`). A query with no words, empty or only whitespace, matches everything.

The words may come in any order and may match inside a longer word (`book` matches `Bookshop`). This is `to_lowercase` and nothing more: `İ` lowercases to `i` followed by U+0307, so `istanbul` does not match `İSTANBUL` while `i̇` does; a whole-string lowercase writes a final `ς` at the end of a word, so `ος` matches `ΟΣ` and `οσ` does not; there is no case folding (`STRASSE` does not match `Straße`) and no Unicode normalization (`e` plus U+0301 does not match a precomposed `é`).

Implement the trait for the two catalogue types in `src/search.rs` (Book ch. 10.2, "Implementing a Trait on a Type"). A `Book`'s search text is its stored title, one ASCII space and its stored author, `format!("{} {}", self.title, self.author)`; both were already cleaned by `Book::new`. A `Member`'s search text is its name exactly as stored, spaces included. Neither overrides `matches`.

Everything LM9 built stays as it was: `fees.rs`, `text.rs`, `member.rs`, `error.rs`, `command.rs` and the menu in `src/main.rs` are unchanged, and so are every LM9 method and its answers. The LM9 regression rows, the LM9 generated suite and the menu transcripts still pass.

**Part 2 · References and the generic `search`**

A blanket implementation makes every reference to a searchable value searchable too: `impl<T: Searchable> Searchable for &T` (Book ch. 10.2, "Using Trait Bounds to Conditionally Implement Methods"). It must forward both methods to the value, `(**self).search_text()` and `(**self).matches(query)` (or `T::matches(*self, query)`). Forwarding `matches` matters: without it, `&T` would use the default and lose a type's own matching rule. Writing `self.matches(query)` inside this `impl` would call the `&T` method itself again, forever, which is why the receiver is dereferenced to the `T` first.

`search` has exactly the signature `pub fn search<'a, T: Searchable>(items: &'a [T], query: &str) -> Vec<&'a T>`. It returns a reference to every item that matches, in slice order, with no sorting and no copies. The results borrow only the items, `'a`, and not the query: a caller may build the query in an inner block and drop it before using the results (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Annotations in Function Signatures"). Elision cannot choose for you here, because there are two input references. The only bound is `T: Searchable`, so a slice of books, of members, of `&Book` (through the blanket implementation) or of a type with nothing but `Searchable` can all be searched. Re-export it at the root with `pub use search::{Searchable, search};`.

**Part 3 · `Display` for `Book`**

In `src/book.rs`, implement `fmt::Display` for `Book` so that `{}` and `to_string()` give the same text as `summary()`, for example `rust by Ada (2024)`, with no final newline: `write!(f, "{}", self.summary())` (Book ch. 10.2, "Implementing a Trait on a Type"; a standard trait may be implemented for `Book` because `Book` is defined in this crate). Add `use std::fmt;` at the top of the file; nothing else in `book.rs` changes.

**Part 4 · `Library::find` and `members_sorted`**

Both methods go in `src/library.rs`, inside `impl Library`, because they read the private fields `books` and `members`: `src/search.rs` is a sibling module and cannot see them. Both return references whose lifetime is elided to that of `&self` (Book ch. 10.3, "Lifetime Elision").

- `find(&self, query: &str) -> Vec<&Book>` returns every stored book whose search text matches the query, in ascending id order. Books are stored in the order they were added and their ids increase from 1, so `search(&self.books, query)` already gives that order; add `search::search` to the `use crate::{…}` list.
- `members_sorted(&self) -> Vec<&Member>` returns every member, smallest id first. A `HashMap` keeps no order (Book ch. 8.3), so copy the ids into a `Vec<u32>`, `sort()` it, and look each id up with `get`.

`find` is a new method beside the LM9 ones. `search_titles` and the `find` command (`execute(Command::Find(…))`) keep their LM9 meaning, a title-only search whose output is `Found: …`; LM10 changes no command output, and a row checks that the two stay distinct.

problems.constraints_md: All LM1–LM9 contracts remain unchanged. At most 100,000 `add_book` calls per `Library` and at most 100,000 members; every text argument and query is valid UTF-8 of at most 100,000 bytes. Member ids use the full `u32` range and years the full `u16` range. No input may make any function panic. No bound names `Clone` or `Copy`, and results are references to stored values, never copies. Chapters 1–10 only: no `unwrap()`, no closures or closure-taking methods, no `dyn`, no `unsafe`, no `impl` of `Iterator`, `From` or an operator trait, and no new menu options. The package is named `library` (edition 2024, no dependencies) and contains exactly `src/lib.rs`, `src/fees.rs`, `src/text.rs`, `src/book.rs`, `src/member.rs`, `src/library.rs`, `src/error.rs`, `src/command.rs`, `src/search.rs` and `src/main.rs`.
hints: Start `src/search.rs` with `use crate::{book::Book, member::Member};` and the trait. The default `matches` is a loop: `let text = self.search_text().to_lowercase(); let query = query.to_lowercase(); for word in query.split_whitespace() { if !text.contains(word) { return false; } } true`.

In `impl<T: Searchable> Searchable for &T`, `self` is a `&&T`, so `(**self)` is the `T`: write `fn matches(&self, query: &str) -> bool { (**self).matches(query) }` and the same for `search_text`. `search` is `let mut out = Vec::new(); for item in items { if item.matches(query) { out.push(item); } } out`, where `item` is already a `&'a T`.

`Display` is `impl fmt::Display for Book { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result { write!(f, "{}", self.summary()) } }`. In `library.rs`, `find` is `search(&self.books, query)`, and `members_sorted` is `let mut ids = Vec::new(); for id in self.members.keys() { ids.push(*id); } ids.sort();` followed by a loop that pushes `self.members.get(&id)` when it is `Some`.
problems.solution_approach_md: `src/search.rs` holds the trait with its default `matches`, the two catalogue implementations, the forwarding implementation for `&T` and the generic `search`, which pushes each matching `&'a T` in slice order. `Book` gains `Display` in its own file by writing its `summary`. The two `Library` queries live beside the private fields they read: `find` hands the stored books to `search`, which keeps their id order, and `members_sorted` sorts the member ids and looks each one up. No LM9 code changes.
problems.idiomatic_md: A trait with one required method and a default turns "searchable" into a capability any type can opt into with a few lines, and the blanket `impl` for `&T` lets the same function search owned values or references without copying either. Signatures carry the borrowing story: `search` names `'a` to promise that results depend on the items alone, while the `Library` methods rely on elision because the only thing they can borrow is the library.
problems.random_md:
Row 31. Reset the generator to seed `0x0A000201` once and generate 300 cases. Each case starts from `Library::new()` and adds nb = 1 + pick(5) books, each drawing its title TT[pick(6)], then its author AU[pick(4)], then its year YR[pick(3)]. It then makes nm = pick(4) `add_member(MI[pick(5)], MN[pick(4)], false)` calls (id drawn first); a repeated id must be rejected with `DuplicateMember`, and an accepted one recorded. Last it draws the query Q[pick(10)]. The lists are TT = `["Rust", " The  Rust Book ", "東京  物語", "İSTANBUL", "ΟΣ", "Straße"]`, AU = `["Ada", " ann lee ", "É", "Bo\u{3000}"]`, YR = `[0, 1965, 65535]`, MI = `[1, 2, 7, 4294967295, 0]`, MN = `["Ann", "Bo Lee", "  ada  ", "東京"]` and Q = `["", "rust", "RUST book", "ada", "lee ann", "i\u{307}", "ος", "STRASSE", "東京", "the rust"]`.

Each case compares with an independent oracle that normalizes each title by splitting it at whitespace itself, trims each author, lowercases texts and queries with `to_lowercase`, splits the query into words by scanning for whitespace characters and tests each word with a byte-by-byte substring search: the ids of `find(query)`; the ids of `members_sorted()` (the accepted ids, sorted); the ids of `crate::search(&l.members_sorted(), query)`, a slice of `&Member` searched through the blanket implementation; and `format!("{}", book)` for every stored book, which must be `title by author (year)`. Realized over the 300 cases: queries 0 to 9 are drawn 31, 39, 30, 28, 30, 31, 23, 32, 32 and 24 times; of the 881 books, 233 match their case's query and 648 do not (by query: 78, 37, 11, 22, 19, 21, 14, 0, 19 and 12 matches, so `STRASSE` never matches `Straße`); of the 359 accepted members 50 match and 309 do not; 42 repeated member ids are rejected; and `find` is empty in 162 cases. The reference solution and the oracle agree on all 300 cases.

Row 34. This is LM9's generated suite (seed `0x09030000`), carried forward unchanged: apply the algorithm and the independent oracle of the LM9 Random tests in Chapter 9's `project.md`. LM10 adds methods and a module but changes no LM9 behaviour, so all 300 command sessions give the same parse results, outputs and catalogue snapshots; the LM10 reference and the LM9 reference produce identical results on all 300.

- Required: exactly `src/lib.rs`, `src/fees.rs`, `src/text.rs`, `src/book.rs`, `src/member.rs`, `src/library.rs`, `src/error.rs`, `src/command.rs`, `src/search.rs` and `src/main.rs`; `src/lib.rs` contains only the eight `pub mod` declarations (without bodies) and the re-exports of LM9 plus `pub use search::{Searchable, search};`.
- Required: `Searchable` declares `search_text` without a body and `matches` with a default body; `src/search.rs` has `impl Searchable for Book`, `impl Searchable for Member` (each defining only `search_text`) and `impl<T: Searchable> Searchable for &T` defining both methods; `search` has the signature `pub fn search<'a, T: Searchable>(items: &'a [T], query: &str) -> Vec<&'a T>`; no bound names `Clone` or `Copy`; `src/book.rs` differs from LM9 only by `impl fmt::Display for Book` (and its `use`), `src/library.rs` only by `members_sorted`, `find` and their `use`, and `src/fees.rs`, `src/text.rs`, `src/member.rs`, `src/error.rs`, `src/command.rs` and `src/main.rs` are unchanged.
- Required: no `unwrap()` call, no closure expression (`|…|`) and no call to `map`, `filter`, `collect`, `sort_by`, `sort_by_key`, `retain`, `any`, `all` or `position` anywhere in the package; no `dyn`, no `unsafe`, no `impl` of `Iterator`, `From` or an operator trait.
problems.notes_md:
Runtime rows use `crate::…` paths, which name the root re-exports of the learner's `src/lib.rs`, rather than `library::…`, for the reason LM8 gives (the crate and its module are both called `library`). The compiler probes (rows 35–38) are compiled as a separate crate that depends on the package, where `library::Book` is unambiguous and nothing is imported: probe 35 relies on that, since a trait method is not callable while the trait is out of scope.

Starter: the LM9 reference compiles without warnings and passes the regression rows 32–34, the menu rows 42–46, the privacy probe 38, probe 35 (with no `matches` anywhere the call is rejected with the same E0599) and rule 41. It fails rows 1–31, because each names `Searchable`, `search`, `find` or `members_sorted` or formats a `Book` with `{}`, none of which exists yet, so those rows do not compile; probes 36 and 37, which are rejected with E0425 (no `search`) instead of the named codes; and rules 39 and 40, which need `src/search.rs`. Part checkpoints, measured, each building without warnings: the Part 1 checkpoint (the trait and its two implementations, re-exporting only `Searchable`) passes rows 1–10 and the regression and menu rows; Part 2 adds the `&T` implementation and `search` and passes rows 1–19; Part 3 adds `Display` and passes rows 1–23; the reference passes every row and both suites. Measured with wrong versions of the reference: matching when any one word is found fails rows 2 and 5 and 37 suite cases; leaving `matches` out of the `&T` implementation fails row 18 and rule 40; not lowercasing the query fails 11 rows; trimming member names fails row 3; dropping the space between title and author fails rows 1, 5, 7 and 10; returning members in `HashMap` order, or largest id first, fails rows 25 and 26; a title-only `find` fails rows 24, 29 and 30; `writeln!` in `Display` fails rows 20–23; switching the `find` command to the new `Library::find` fails row 29 and rule 40; treating an empty query as matching nothing fails rows 4, 9, 19 and 28; and reversing the results of `search` fails rows 11–15, 24, 28 and 30. Row 10 is the `large` row (a 99,999-byte title) and row 26 inserts 1,000 members in scrambled order; both run in a few milliseconds in a debug build.

The running-project contract adds `Library::find` without changing `execute(Command::Find)`, so the command keeps LM9's title-only output (row 29 records the difference); a later milestone may switch the command to `find`, and that change will be stated there. The public API cannot store books out of id order, so `find`'s "ascending id" order is the storage order and needs no sort.
